cards.a: j'avais, tu avais, il/elle avait, nous avions, vous aviez, ils/elles avaient
cards.n: Built regularly on nous avons, unlike être. Avais and avait sound identical, so only the spelling separates them.

cards.q: Conjugue 'aller' au futur simple (toutes les personnes).
cards.a: j'irai, tu iras, il/elle ira, nous irons, vous irez, ils/elles iront
cards.n: Do not slide into j'irais, which is the conditional. Every future form keeps an r before its ending.

cards.q: Conjugue 'faire' au futur simple (toutes les personnes).
cards.a: je ferai, tu feras, il/elle fera, nous ferons, vous ferez, ils/elles feront
cards.n: The stem fer- drops the ai of faire, so je ferai never has an a. Refaire follows: je referai.

cards.q: Conjugue 'venir' au futur simple (toutes les personnes).
cards.a: je viendrai, tu viendras, il/elle viendra, nous viendrons, vous viendrez, ils/elles viendront
cards.n: The stem viendr- adds a d that the infinitive does not have, exactly like tenir, which gives tiendr-.

cards.q: Conjugue 'être' au conditionnel présent (toutes les personnes).
cards.a: je serais, tu serais, il/elle serait, nous serions, vous seriez, ils/elles seraient
cards.n: Je serais and je serai differ by a single letter and sound almost identical, a classic dictée and writing trap.

cards.q: Conjugue 'avoir' au conditionnel présent (toutes les personnes).
cards.a: j'aurais, tu aurais, il/elle aurait, nous aurions, vous auriez, ils/elles auraient
cards.n: The stem aur- is the one used for the futur simple; only the endings, taken from the imparfait, change.

cards.q: Conjugue 'venir' au passé composé (toutes les personnes).
cards.a: je suis venu(e), tu es venu(e), il/elle est venu(e), nous sommes venu(e)s, vous êtes venu(e)(s), ils/elles sont venu(e)s
cards.n: venir is a DR & MRS VANDERTRAMP verb: it takes être and its participle agrees with the subject — unlike the majority of verbs, which take avoir and show no subject agreement.

cards.q: Cite huit verbes ou expressions qui expriment le doute, la volonté, l'émotion ou la nécessité et qui déclenchent le subjonctif.
cards.a: douter que, vouloir que, souhaiter que, avoir peur que, être content que, regretter que, il faut que, il est nécessaire que.
cards.n: Complements the conjunctions list: here the trigger is the main-clause verb's meaning, not a conjunction.

cards.q: Énonce la règle du subjonctif après un superlatif ou des expressions comme 'le seul', 'le premier', 'le dernier'.
cards.a: When the superlative or these restrictive expressions introduce a subjective judgment rather than an objective fact, the relative clause takes the subjunctive: c'est le seul film qui soit vraiment original.
cards.n: If the statement is presented as a plain fact instead of an opinion, the indicative is also possible.

cards.q: Contraste 'après que' et 'avant que' quant au mode employé.
cards.a: après que is followed by the indicative, since the action is a real, completed fact: après qu'il est parti. avant que is followed by the subjunctive, often with an optional ne explétif: avant qu'il ne parte.
cards.n: Many native speakers use the subjunctive after après que too, but the exam expects the indicative.

cards.q: Complète au subjonctif : 'Il faut que tu (finir) ton travail avant ce soir.'
cards.a: que tu finisses. il faut que is one of the most common impersonal triggers of the subjunctive.
cards.n: Il faut que triggers the subjunctive, but il faut on its own takes a bare infinitive: il faut finir ce soir.

cards.q: Décide : indicatif ou subjonctif après 'espérer que' ?
cards.a: Indicative: j'espère qu'il viendra. Despite meaning 'to hope', espérer que behaves like a verb of certainty, not of doubt or wish, and is a well-known exception among verbs of desire.
cards.n: A classic trap: souhaiter que takes the subjunctive, but espérer que does not.

cards.q: Explique la formation et l'emploi du passé récent.
cards.a: venir de + infinitive expresses an action that has just happened: je viens de manger (I just ate). At the imperfect, venir de + infinitive expresses an action that had just happened: je venais de manger quand le téléphone a sonné.
cards.n: Distinct from le futur proche (aller + infinitif), which looks forward instead of back.

cards.q: Reconnais le passé simple : associe 'il fut', 'il eut', 'il fit', 'il alla' à leurs infinitifs.
cards.a: il fut → être, il eut → avoir, il fit → faire, il alla → aller. These irregular third-person forms appear constantly in literary narration and fairy tales.
cards.n: Il alla is the only regular form of the four, since -er verbs always take -a in the third person singular.

cards.q: Reconnais le passé simple : associe 'il vint', 'il vit', 'il put', 'il voulut' à leurs infinitifs.
cards.a: il vint → venir, il vit → voir, il put → pouvoir, il voulut → vouloir.
cards.n: Il vit is ambiguous out of context: it is also the present of vivre, he lives. The surrounding tense decides.

cards.q: Conjugue 'parler' au passé simple (toutes les personnes).
cards.a: je parlai, tu parlas, il/elle parla, nous parlâmes, vous parlâtes, ils/elles parlèrent
cards.n: The circumflex on parlâmes and parlâtes marks this tense; the imparfait would give parlions and parliez.

cards.q: Donne les terminaisons du passé simple pour les verbes réguliers en -ir et -re à la troisième personne (singulier et pluriel).
cards.a: -it for il/elle (il finit, il vendit), -irent for ils/elles (ils finirent, ils vendirent).
cards.n: This is why passé simple is sometimes missed entirely: the il/elle form for -ir verbs looks identical to the present tense (il finit is both present and passé simple), a silent trap that only context in a literary text can resolve. -re verbs do not have this overlap: present il vend versus passé simple il vendit are visibly different.

cards.q: Pourquoi n'a-t-on pas besoin de conjuguer le passé simple à l'oral ni de le produire à l'examen AP ?
cards.a: It is a purely literary, written tense reserved for narration in novels, tales and formal history texts; nobody uses it in conversation. On the AP exam you only need to recognize it while reading, never to produce it in speaking or writing.
cards.n: The third-person forms are the ones you actually meet: il fut, il eut, il fit, ils furent, ils firent.

cards.q: Explique la construction 'verbe de perception + infinitif' avec voir, entendre, regarder, écouter.
cards.a: These perception verbs are followed directly by an infinitive with no preposition, and the infinitive can come before or after its own subject: Je vois les enfants jouer / Je vois jouer les enfants (I see the children playing).
cards.n: Laisser behaves the same way; faire also takes a bare infinitive, but the infinitive must come right after it: je fais jouer les enfants. English uses an -ing form here, which has no French counterpart.

cards.q: Complète : 'J'entends les oiseaux ___ (chanter) chaque matin.'
cards.a: chanter. Entendre + infinitive needs no preposition: j'entends les oiseaux chanter.
cards.n: Do not slip in a de or an à; that reflex comes from verbs like demander de and commencer à.

cards.q: Complète, puis donne les deux ordres possibles : 'Elle a regardé ___ (partir) le train.'
cards.a: Elle a regardé partir le train. or Elle a regardé le train partir. Both orders are correct with a perception verb; only a pronoun cannot separate the two verbs: elle l'a regardé partir, not elle a regardé le partir.
cards.n: This pronoun-placement rule also applies to laisser + infinitive: elle l'a laissé partir.

cards.q: Contraste 'écouter quelqu'un parler' et 'écouter quelqu'un qui parle'.
cards.a: Both are correct and mean roughly the same thing. 'Écouter quelqu'un parler' uses the perception-verb-plus-infinitive construction directly. 'Écouter quelqu'un qui parle' uses a relative clause instead and is slightly more explicit or formal.
cards.n: Écouter and entendre are not interchangeable: entendre is passive hearing, écouter is deliberate listening.

cards.q: Explique la construction du faire causatif (faire + infinitif).
cards.a: Faire + infinitive means to have or make someone do something, or to have something done: Je fais réparer ma voiture (I have my car repaired, I'm having someone repair my car). The person doing the action, if named, follows the infinitive, or is introduced with à or par.
cards.n: Do not confuse it with laisser plus infinitive, which means to let someone do rather than to make them do.

cards.q: Complète : 'Le professeur fait ___ (écrire) une rédaction aux élèves.'
cards.a: écrire. Faire + infinitive: le professeur fait écrire une rédaction aux élèves (the teacher has the students write an essay).
cards.n: The infinitive after faire never agrees and never turns into a past participle, whatever the tense of faire.

cards.q: Complète en utilisant le faire causatif : 'Je (couper) mes cheveux chez le coiffeur.'
cards.a: Je fais couper mes cheveux chez le coiffeur, or more idiomatically je me fais couper les cheveux (I get my hair cut at the hairdresser's). Faire + infinitive expresses having something done to you, not doing it yourself.
cards.n: This is the single most common everyday use of the causative: talking about services done to you (couper les cheveux, réparer la voiture, nettoyer les vêtements).

cards.q: Contraste 'je répare ma voiture' et 'je fais réparer ma voiture'.
cards.a: 'Je répare ma voiture' means I repair the car myself. 'Je fais réparer ma voiture' means I have someone else repair it for me: the causative faire shifts the doer of the action away from the subject.
cards.n: In this construction a preceding direct object never triggers agreement: la voiture que j'ai fait réparer.

cards.q: Contraste 'venir de', 'être en train de' et 'être sur le point de' + infinitif.
cards.a: Venir de + infinitive = just did something: je viens de manger (I just ate). Être en train de + infinitive = in the middle of doing something: je suis en train de manger (I'm eating right now). Être sur le point de + infinitive = about to do something: je suis sur le point de manger (I'm about to eat).
cards.n: Only venir de is restricted in tense: it works in the present and the imparfait, never in the passé composé.

cards.q: Complète : 'Ne le dérange pas, il ___ (être) en train de dormir.'
cards.a: est. Il est en train de dormir describes an action in progress at this moment.
cards.n: The plain present would also work here: il dort. The periphrasis only adds the insistence on right now.

cards.q: Complète : 'Dépêchons-nous, le film ___ (être) sur le point de commencer.'
cards.a: est. Le film est sur le point de commencer expresses an action about to happen very soon.
cards.n: Point stays singular and the de before the infinitive is compulsory. Aller plus infinitive is the everyday synonym.

cards.q: Mets au passé, puis explique le sens : 'Il vient de partir.'
cards.a: Il venait de partir (imparfait), meaning he had just left, a moment before another past event. Venir de shifts to the imparfait, not the passé composé, to express a recent past within a past narration.
cards.n: This shift to the imparfait for a past 'just did' is easy to forget under time pressure, since venir de otherwise pairs so naturally with the present.

cards.q: Explique pourquoi 'être en train de' ne s'emploie généralement pas pour une action future imminente.
cards.a: Être en train de describes an action actually in progress, so it clashes with the future; for an action about to happen, French uses être sur le point de or aller + infinitive instead: il va commencer / il est sur le point de commencer, not 'il sera en train de commencer'.
cards.n: French has no continuous tense, so this periphrasis is the only way to insist that an action is under way.

cards.q: Conjugue 'parler' au plus-que-parfait (toutes les personnes).
cards.a: j'avais parlé, tu avais parlé, il/elle avait parlé, nous avions parlé, vous aviez parlé, ils/elles avaient parlé
cards.n: Same auxiliary + participle pattern as the passé composé, just with avoir/être in the imparfait instead of the présent.

cards.q: Mets au futur proche : 'Nous partons en vacances.'
cards.a: Nous allons partir en vacances. Aller au présent + infinitif expresses a near or planned future, just like English 'going to'.
cards.n: Aller stays in the present: nous allons partir. With aller itself you get nous allons aller, which is correct.

cards.q: Conjugue 'aller' au conditionnel passé (toutes les personnes).
cards.a: je serais allé(e), tu serais allé(e), il/elle serait allé(e), nous serions allé(e)s, vous seriez allé(e)(s), ils/elles seraient allé(e)s
cards.n: Aller takes être, so the past participle agrees with the subject, just like in the passé composé.

cards.q: Conjugue 'faire' au subjonctif passé (toutes les personnes).
cards.a: que j'aie fait, que tu aies fait, qu'il/elle ait fait, que nous ayons fait, que vous ayez fait, qu'ils/elles aient fait
cards.n: Only the auxiliary moves into the subjunctive; the past participle stays exactly as it is in the passé composé.

cards.q: Donne le participe présent de 'être', 'savoir' et 'avoir' - les trois exceptions à la règle générale.
cards.a: étant, sachant, ayant. Every other verb builds its present participle from the nous-form stem (nous parlons → parlant; nous faisons → faisant), but these three are irregular.
cards.n: Sachant and ayant are rare outside writing, while étant turns up constantly in étant donné que, given that.

cards.q: Traduis en utilisant le gérondif : 'She hurt herself while cooking.'
cards.a: Elle s'est blessée en cuisinant. En + present participle expresses the simultaneous circumstance 'while doing something'.
cards.n: En is the only preposition that takes a present participle; every other one takes the infinitive, as in avant de partir.

cards.q: Complète : 'Après (finir) ses devoirs, il a regardé la télé.'
cards.a: Après avoir fini ses devoirs, il a regardé la télé. 'Après' + infinitive always requires the past infinitive (avoir/être + participle) to show the action happened first.
cards.n: A frequent written error is 'après finir' - après can never be followed by a bare infinitive.

cards.q: Mets à la voix passive : 'Les élèves ont écrit cette lettre.'
cards.a: Cette lettre a été écrite par les élèves. The auxiliary être is conjugated in the same tense as the active verb (here, passé composé), and the participle agrees with the new subject.
cards.n: Only transitive verbs, those with a direct object, can be made passive - a sentence like 'il a plu' has no passive form.

cards.q: State the two sections of the redesigned AP French Language and Culture exam and their weights.
cards.a: Section I is free response and counts 50%: Project Presentation 20%, Project Q&A 15%, Argumentative Essay 15%. Section II is multiple choice and counts 50%: Listening 25% and Reading 25%.
cards.n: Two of the three free-response tasks are built around your own project, so preparation you do in advance is worth 35% of the exam.

cards.q: State the three tasks in Section I and what each one measures.
cards.a: 1) Project Presentation (20%) - presentational speaking about your own researched project; 2) Project Q&A (15%) - interpersonal speaking, answering questions about that project; 3) Argumentative Essay (15%) - presentational writing from three sources.
cards.n: Two of the three tasks are speaking, and both draw on the same project. One strong project carries 35% of your score.

cards.q: State what changes about the exam's delivery and when.
cards.a: The exam becomes fully digital in Bluebook beginning with the May 2027 administration: multiple choice, audio, and typed and recorded responses all run inside the app.
cards.n: Practice typing French accents on the device you will use; hunting for é under time pressure costs real points.

cards.q: Define the Personalized Project Reference and give its deadline.
cards.a: The PPR is the reference document you build for the Course Project and submit through the AP Digital Portfolio by April 30. The theme is set by the College Board, not by you: a Course Project Packet — a prompt plus six to eight authentic Francophone sources — is released each January, and the May 2027 project comes from Thème 3, l’art et la créativité, focused on music. You personalise the Francophone region or community and the angle. The PPR is the shared basis for both the Project Presentation and the Project Q&A on exam day.
cards.h: → what it is, who sets the theme, the deadline
cards.n: The two tasks built on it are 35% of the score, and missing the April 30 submission leaves you with nothing to present from. Treat it as a hard deadline.

cards.q: Explain what makes a strong Personalized Project Reference.
cards.a: A narrow, arguable question inside the assigned prompt from the January packet, personalised to one Francophone region or community; sources from the Francophone world, not translations, going beyond the packet with your own research; concrete data, examples and vocabulary you can actually deploy; and cues — key words, figures, names — rather than a written-out script.
cards.n: The PPR is a launchpad, not a speech. If you can only read it aloud, you cannot survive the Q&A.

cards.q: State the length of the Project Presentation and how to structure it.
cards.a: About three minutes of continuous speech. Structure: a hook and your guiding question (about 20 seconds), the cultural context (40 seconds), two or three developed points with evidence (about 90 seconds), and a conclusion that answers your question and connects to a broader Francophone context (30 seconds).
cards.n: Rehearse with a timer. Running short leaves obvious silence; running long gets you cut off mid-argument.

cards.q: Explain how to fill three minutes without repeating yourself.
cards.a: Plan three distinct blocks, each with its own example and its own vocabulary field. Use signposting (tout d'abord, ensuite, enfin) so the listener hears the structure, add one comparison to your own community, and reserve one anecdote or statistic you can expand if you are running short.
cards.n: Padding by repeating your thesis in three ways is transparent. A held-in-reserve example is the safer insurance.

cards.q: State the format of the Project Q&A and the time you get per answer.
cards.a: You hear questions about your project and record a response to each, with roughly 40 seconds per answer. The questions probe your reasoning, your sources and your personal connection, not just the facts you presented.
cards.n: 40 seconds is about 80-100 words: enough for a direct answer, one reason and one example. Plan for exactly that shape.

cards.q: State the three-move template for a 40-second Q&A response.
cards.a: 1) Answer directly in the first sentence, reusing the question's key words (5-8 seconds). 2) Give one reason with a connector - parce que, en effet, c'est pourquoi (15 seconds). 3) Add a concrete example from your project or your own life, then a one-clause close (15-20 seconds).
cards.n: Answer first. Candidates who narrate their way toward an answer run out of time before they give one.

cards.q: Explain what to do if you do not understand a Q&A question or go blank.
cards.a: Never stay silent. Start with a filler that buys time and sounds native - C'est une bonne question... / Si je comprends bien, vous me demandez si... / Ce qui me vient à l'esprit, c'est... - then reframe the question toward the part of your project you know best and answer that.
cards.n: Silence scores nothing; a partially off-target but fluent answer still earns language points.

cards.q: State what the Argumentative Essay task provides and roughly how the time is divided.
cards.a: Three sources on one theme: two print (usually an article and a chart, table or infographic) and one audio played twice. You get a reading and listening period of roughly fifteen minutes, then about forty minutes to write.
cards.n: Confirm exact timings in the current CED, but plan on the 15/40 split: annotate while reading, do not wait until the clock starts on writing.

cards.q: State the four-part structure of a high-scoring argumentative essay.
cards.a: 1) Introduction: present the theme, state the question, and give a clear thesis. 2) Body paragraph(s) developing your position with evidence cited from the sources. 3) A paragraph acknowledging the counterargument and refuting it. 4) Conclusion that restates the thesis in new terms and opens onto a broader perspective.
cards.n: A visible counterargument paragraph is the single clearest sophistication signal available to you.

cards.q: Explain why you must cite all three sources and what happens if you do not.
cards.a: The task explicitly requires you to integrate all three sources. Ignoring one - almost always the audio or the chart - caps your score on the content dimension no matter how good your French is.
cards.n: Take at least two notes on the audio during each of its two playings. That is the source students most often drop.

cards.q: Give the French formulas for citing each of the three sources.
cards.a: Print article: Selon la source numéro 1, ... / D'après l'auteur de l'article, ... Chart or table: Le tableau de la source numéro 2 montre que... / Les chiffres indiquent que... Audio: Dans l'enregistrement, l'intervenant affirme que... / Selon la source audio, ...
cards.n: Name the source and paraphrase; never copy a whole sentence. Lifted language earns no credit for your own control.

cards.q: Write a French sentence that cites a chart AND interprets it, rather than only describing it.
cards.a: Le tableau de la source numéro 2 révèle que le nombre d'utilisateurs a doublé en cinq ans, ce qui confirme que cette pratique n'est plus marginale.
cards.n: Data plus a ce qui clause. Description alone reads as summary; the interpretation is what earns evidence credit.

cards.q: Explain how to handle a source that contradicts your thesis.
cards.a: Cite it openly, concede the valid part, then limit it: Certes, la source numéro 3 souligne que... Toutefois, cet argument néglige le fait que... Turning the contradiction into your counterargument paragraph converts a weakness into evidence of nuance.
cards.n: Pretending a source does not exist is worse than disagreeing with it; graders are reading for engagement with all three.

cards.q: State how to write the thesis sentence of the argumentative essay.
cards.a: One sentence, at the end of the introduction, that answers the question directly and previews your line of argument: Nous soutiendrons que les réseaux sociaux renforcent l'engagement civique des jeunes, malgré les risques qu'ils comportent.
cards.n: A thesis that merely announces the topic (Je vais parler de...) scores nothing. It must take a position.

cards.q: State what graders reward in the free-response tasks.
cards.a: Task completion and development of ideas; range and precision of vocabulary; control of grammar and syntax with a variety of tenses and structures; organization and use of connectors; register appropriate to the audience; and for speaking, pronunciation, intonation and fluency.
cards.n: Accuracy alone does not maximize your score. Simple, error-free French sits in the middle band; range is what lifts it.

cards.q: Explain how to control register across the three free-response tasks.
cards.a: The essay and presentation are formal presentational French: vous, full negation with ne, inversion or est-ce que for questions, no slang, no anglicisms, no contractions like t'as. The Q&A is interpersonal but still academic: keep vous, but shorter sentences and natural fillers are appropriate.
cards.n: Dropping ne (je sais pas) is normal speech but is penalized in a formal presentation. Keep it in.

cards.q: State four anglicisms or informal habits to eliminate from your exam French.
cards.a: 1) Dropping ne in negation; 2) using ça in formal writing where cela is expected; 3) English-modeled prepositions (chercher pour, demander pour, entrer dans le train); 4) false friends such as actuellement (currently, not actually), éventuellement (possibly, not eventually) and assister à (to attend, not to assist).
cards.n: False friends are graded as vocabulary errors and can distort your whole argument.

cards.q: Explain how to work the listening portion of Section II.
cards.a: Read the questions during the preview time and turn them into what to listen for. On the first playing, capture the gist, the speakers and the register; on the second, hunt the specific details the questions ask about. Answer from what was said, not from what is plausible.
cards.n: Distractors are built from words you actually hear in the wrong relationship. Recognizing a word is not the same as it being the answer.

cards.q: Explain how to work the reading portion of Section II.
cards.a: Read the introduction line first - it names the source, date and context and often answers a question outright. Skim for structure, then read the questions, then reread targeted paragraphs. Use the surrounding sentence, not your dictionary memory, to infer unfamiliar vocabulary.
cards.n: Questions about the author's purpose or intended audience are usually answerable from the introduction line alone.

cards.q: State a minute-by-minute plan for the forty-minute essay writing period.
cards.a: Minutes 1-5: outline - thesis, two arguments with the source that supports each, and the counterargument. Minutes 6-33: write, cutting nothing you planned. Minutes 34-40: proofread for verb endings, agreement, accents, and check that all three sources are named.
cards.n: The five-minute outline is what makes the counterargument paragraph actually get written instead of being crowded out.

cards.q: State the five-point proofreading checklist for written French under time pressure.
cards.a: 1) Every verb has a subject it agrees with; 2) past participles agree where required; 3) adjectives agree in gender and number; 4) accents are present, especially e-acute endings and a versus a-grave; 5) all three sources are cited by name.
cards.n: Run the checklist as five separate passes, not one. Looking for one error type at a time actually catches them.

cards.q: Donne quatre formules de haut niveau pour introduire un sujet ou une problématique.
cards.a: Il convient de s'interroger sur... / La question qui se pose est de savoir si... / Ce sujet soulève un débat qui divise... / À l'heure actuelle, ...
cards.n: Opening with a question rather than an announcement immediately sets an argumentative frame.

cards.q: Donne quatre formules de haut niveau pour présenter une source.
cards.a: Selon la source numéro 1, ... / D'après le tableau, ... / L'auteur de l'article soutient que... / Dans l'enregistrement, l'intervenant explique que...
cards.n: Vary the verb: soutient, affirme, souligne, révèle, nuance. Repeating dit four times reads as thin vocabulary.

cards.q: Donne quatre formules de haut niveau pour marquer une opposition ou une concession.
cards.a: Certes, ... mais... / En revanche, ... / Il n'en demeure pas moins que... / Si l'on peut admettre que..., il n'en reste pas moins que...
cards.n: Il n'en demeure pas moins que is a memorized, high-value hinge for the counterargument paragraph.

cards.q: Donne quatre formules de haut niveau pour renforcer ou illustrer un argument.
cards.a: En effet, ... / À titre d'exemple, ... / Cela se vérifie notamment lorsque... / Il suffit de penser à... pour s'en convaincre.
cards.n: en effet confirms what you just said; en fait corrects it. They are not interchangeable.

cards.q: Donne cinq formules de haut niveau pour conclure.
cards.a: En somme, ... / Force est de constater que... / Tout bien considéré, ... / Il ressort de cette analyse que... / Reste à savoir si...
cards.n: Reste à savoir si... lets you end on an open question, which reads as sophistication rather than repetition.

cards.q: Donne quatre formules pour gagner du temps à l'oral sans rester silencieux.
cards.a: C'est une excellente question... / Ce qui me vient immédiatement à l'esprit, c'est... / Si je comprends bien votre question, ... / Permettez-moi de préciser un point...
cards.n: These are real French discourse markers, not filler noise like euh. They buy three seconds and raise your register.

cards.q: Donne quatre formules pour comparer ta communauté à celle évoquée dans les sources de l'essai argumentatif.
cards.a: De la même manière que..., ... / Contrairement à ce qu'on observe ici, ... / À la différence de..., chez nous... / Tout comme dans la source, on constate que...
cards.n: Comparing your own community to the sources is exactly the personal connection graders reward in the Q&A too.

cards.q: State, in general terms, what separates a top-band response from a low-band response on the free-response tasks.
cards.a: Top-band responses fully complete the task with well-developed, nuanced ideas, a wide and precise vocabulary, and varied structures, with only minor errors. Low-band responses are underdeveloped or off-task, rely on repetitive simple language, and contain errors that obscure meaning.
cards.n: Going off-task is the harshest trap, since answering a different prompt caps the score whatever the language is like.

cards.q: Rewrite this flat opening as an engaging hook: 'Aujourd'hui, je vais parler de l'immigration.'
cards.a: Imaginez quitter votre pays sans savoir si vous y retournerez un jour : c'est la réalité de millions de personnes aujourd'hui, et le sujet de mon projet.
cards.n: A concrete scenario or question draws the listener in far better than announcing the topic.

cards.q: Explain how to keep Project Q&A answers consistent with your Personalized Project Reference without sounding memorized.
cards.a: Know your facts and vocabulary cold, but build each answer freshly around the question asked rather than reciting a fixed paragraph. Reusing key words from the question and adding one small new detail each time keeps answers grounded yet natural.
cards.n: The PPR stays in front of you during the Q&A, so glance at a cue instead of reciting a paragraph from memory.

cards.q: State what the Personalized Project Reference should NOT contain.
cards.a: No fully written-out sentences meant to be read aloud, and no complete script or essay - only key words, figures, names and structure cues that support spontaneous speech.
cards.n: Treating the PPR as a script to memorize is the single most common way students undermine their Q&A.

cards.q: State how to handle passé simple verb forms if they appear in an AP reading passage.
cards.a: Treat them exactly like the passé composé in meaning, a completed past action (il dit = he said, elle prit = she took), and keep moving; you are only ever asked to recognize them, never to produce the passé simple yourself.
cards.n: The forms to spot are the ones with no obvious infinitive: il fut, il eut, il fit, il put, il vint, ils furent.

cards.q: Decide: for the Project Q&A and any interpersonal task, what register should you default to, and when should you break from it?
cards.a: Default to vous and a neutral-to-formal register: full negation with ne, est-ce que or inversion for questions, no slang. Break from it only if the prompt explicitly establishes an informal relationship, such as writing to a close friend.
cards.n: Dropping the ne is the commonest lapse: say je ne pense pas, not je pense pas, even in the spoken tasks.

cards.q: State a common trap involving time expressions on the listening section, and how to avoid it.
cards.a: French audio routinely states times on the 24-hour clock: dix-neuf heures means 7 PM, not 9 AM. Convert on the fly, subtracting 12 from anything over 12, instead of assuming AM or PM from context.
cards.n: Drill the forms announcements actually use: dix-huit heures trente, vingt et une heures, zéro heure trente.

cards.q: Fix the agreement error and explain it: 'La plupart des Français pense que le télétravail améliore la qualité de vie.'
cards.a: pensent, not pense. The verb agrees with the plural noun that follows 'la plupart des' (Français), not with the singular word 'plupart' itself.
cards.n: This exact error, a singular verb after la plupart des, is one of the most common agreement slips in student essays.

cards.q: Write a formal-register sentence using the causative faire to argue that a government 'should have bike lanes built'.
cards.a: Le gouvernement devrait faire construire davantage de pistes cyclables. Faire + infinitive, rather than construire alone, correctly shows the government commissioning the work rather than building it itself: precise and appropriately formal for policy argumentation.
cards.n: Devoir in the conditional turns a demand into advice, which suits policy argument far better than il faut.

cards.q: Decide, from context: in 'Il assiste à la conférence chaque année,' does 'assiste' mean 'assists' or 'attends'?
cards.a: Attends. Assister à means to attend an event, not to help: a classic faux ami. A reading-comprehension distractor may tempt you toward 'assists', but à la conférence confirms attendance, not assistance.
cards.n: The verb that really means to help is aider, while une assistance does mean help, which keeps the trap alive.

cards.q: Donne trois formules de haut niveau pour nuancer une opinion sans l'abandonner complètement.
cards.a: Il n'empêche que... / Cela dit, ... / Il n'en reste pas moins que...
cards.n: All three take the indicative, not the subjunctive, even though they feel concessive like bien que.

cards.q: Cite trois mots utiles pour un essai sur les défis mondiaux, un par domaine : le numérique, l'environnement, la santé.
cards.a: le cyberharcèlement (numérique) / le gaspillage alimentaire (environnement) / la sécurité sociale (santé).
cards.n: Pair each noun with a verb you can actually deploy: lutter contre le gaspillage, signaler le cyberharcèlement.

cards.q: Decide: it is minute 15 of the 40-minute essay period and you have just finished annotating all three sources. What should you be doing right now?
cards.a: Writing your thesis statement and a quick outline of your three body paragraphs. By minute 15 you should be moving from reading into planning, so you still have 20+ minutes left to draft.
cards.n: The prompt itself supplies the question to answer, so the thesis should echo its wording rather than invent a new topic.

cards.q: State why you should write your thesis statement before drafting body paragraphs, even under time pressure.
cards.a: The thesis anchors every paragraph that follows; writing it first prevents you from wandering off-topic and having to rewrite paragraphs later, which costs far more time than the 30 seconds it takes to write one clear sentence.
cards.n: Essays without a clear, locatable thesis lose points even when the French is grammatically strong.

cards.q: Your Project Presentation recording is almost over and you have not yet reached your conclusion. State the fastest way to close strongly in one sentence.
cards.a: Circle back to your opening idea or thesis in a single synthesizing sentence, such as 'Voilà pourquoi je pense que...' A one-sentence callback reads as intentional, unlike simply stopping mid-thought.
cards.n: Prepare that callback in advance alongside your hook, so the two bookend each other whatever you had to cut.

cards.q: Decide: for the Project Q&A, should you pause silently to think before answering, or start speaking right away while you organize your thought?
cards.a: Start speaking right away, using a transitional phrase like 'C'est une bonne question...' or 'Alors, en ce qui concerne...' while you finish forming your answer. Dead air costs you more than a slightly loose opening sentence.
cards.n: Interpersonal speaking is scored partly on how naturally the exchange flows - silence reads as a breakdown in communication.

cards.q: State the two agreement checks worth doing first when proofreading a French paragraph, and why those two before anything else.
cards.a: Subject-verb agreement and noun-adjective/article gender-number agreement. These two error types are the most frequent in student writing and the fastest to scan for, so checking them first catches the most points for the least time.
cards.n: Scan for the -s and -e endings in particular: they carry both agreements and are silent, so the ear never flags them.

cards.q: Proofread and correct: 'Les fille sont aller à la bibliothèque hier.'
cards.a: Les filles sont allées à la bibliothèque hier. Three fixes: filles needs a plural -s, the participle allé must agree with the feminine plural subject (allées), and aller takes être as its auxiliary.
cards.n: Aller belongs to the être verbs, the group usually memorised as la maison d'être or DR MRS VANDERTRAMP.

cards.q: Decide: proofreading under time pressure - read silently in your head, or mouth the words as if speaking? Which catches more errors?
cards.a: Mouthing the words. Reading purely in your head lets your brain autocorrect missing endings and awkward phrasing; forcing yourself to mentally 'say' each word slows you down just enough to notice a missing verb ending or a clunky sentence.
cards.n: Silent endings are the reason: parle, parles and parlent sound alike, so only the eye catches the difference.

cards.q: State what you should do in the seconds before an audio recording begins, once you can see the questions.
cards.a: Preview every question and answer choice. Knowing what to listen for turns the task from decoding French from scratch into confirming which choice matches what you already expect to hear.
cards.n: The same habit pays on the reading section, where the questions usually follow the order of the passage.

cards.q: Decide: during the listening section, you miss a detail and the audio only plays once. What is the best use of the next few seconds?
cards.a: Keep listening forward. Mark your best guess for the missed question and move on immediately - dwelling on what you missed means missing the next answer too, turning one lost point into several.
cards.n: Guessing at once also keeps your answers aligned with the numbering; a blank left for later is how slips start.

cards.q: State a common distractor pattern in listening multiple-choice questions, and a strategy to avoid falling for it.
cards.a: An answer choice repeats a word verbatim from the audio but distorts its actual meaning or context. Listen for the relationship between ideas, not for word-matching - the right answer often paraphrases the audio rather than quoting it.
cards.n: Test writers deliberately plant a familiar-sounding wrong answer to catch students who skim for keywords instead of following meaning.

cards.q: State the order in which to read a reading-section passage and its questions for the most efficient use of time.
cards.a: Skim the title, source line, and the questions first, then read the passage actively looking for those specific answers. Reading the questions cold after the passage means rereading the whole text to hunt for evidence.
cards.n: Read the line naming the source and date as well, since some questions ask about audience or purpose.

cards.q: From context, does 'réaliser' in 'Elle a pu enfin réaliser son rêve d'ouvrir sa boutique' mean 'to realize' or 'to fulfill'?
cards.a: To fulfill/achieve. Réaliser un rêve means to make a dream come true, not to become aware of it - another classic faux ami that a distractor answer may exploit.
cards.n: Pair this with 'assister à' and 'attendre' as the three reading-section faux amis most likely to appear.

cards.q: Decide: for a question about the author's tone, is one strong adjective or a pattern across the whole passage more reliable evidence?
cards.a: A pattern across the whole passage. One vivid word can be an outlier or even ironic; tone questions reward noticing the cumulative pattern of word choice, not a single data point.
cards.n: The French words for this are le ton and le registre, and both turn up in the question stems themselves.

cards.q: Explain why a grammatically simple but fully accurate response can outscore a complex response full of errors.
cards.a: Graders reward successful communication first: a simple, accurate response gets your message across cleanly, while frequent errors can obscure meaning and pull the score down even if the vocabulary is ambitious. The ideal is accuracy AND sophistication, but accuracy comes first.
cards.n: Aim for controlled range: one subjunctive and one relative clause you are sure of beat five you are not.

cards.q: Decide: you don't know the exact French word you need mid-sentence during the Project Q&A. Should you stop and search for it, or talk around it?
cards.a: Talk around it - use circumlocution. Describe the idea with words you do know rather than freezing; keeping the communication flowing is scored more favorably than a long silent pause while you search your memory.
cards.n: Circumlocution is itself a tested communication strategy - graders can see it as a strength, not just a workaround.

cards.q: State which two of the exam's five tasks are recorded speaking tasks, and which three are not.
cards.a: Recorded speaking: the Project Presentation and the Project Q&A. Not recorded speaking: the Argumentative Essay (written), Listening and Reading (multiple choice).
cards.n: Both speaking tasks rest on your own project, so one well-chosen topic carries you through a quarter of the exam.

cards.q: Explain why the Project Presentation and Project Q&A are graded on similar rubric dimensions even though one is prepared and the other is spontaneous.
cards.a: Both tasks assess the same underlying skills - task completion, language use, and comprehensibility - just under different conditions. The rubric rewards effective communication regardless of how much preparation you had, so spontaneity is never an excuse graders factor in.
cards.n: Rehearsing the presentation aloud also trains the Q&A, since both draw on the same stock of vocabulary.

cards.q: Rewrite as terse keyword cues, not a full sentence: 'Je vais parler de comment les jeunes Français utilisent les réseaux sociaux pour militer.'
cards.a: jeunes Français / réseaux sociaux / militantisme. Cues should be a handful of words that jog your memory, not a script you could read aloud.
cards.n: The PPR allows only words and short phrases, never full sentences, so keyword form is a rule and not just a tactic.

cards.q: Decide: should you memorize your Project Presentation word-for-word, or memorize its structure and key phrases? Justify your choice.
cards.a: Memorize the structure and key phrases, not the exact words. A word-for-word script increases the risk of going completely blank if you lose your place, and a recited delivery sounds flatter than one built from a flexible outline.
cards.n: Graders can often tell the difference between a memorized script and a genuinely spoken response - the latter tends to sound more natural even with small hesitations.

cards.q: Rewrite in a more formal register appropriate for the Argumentative Essay: 'Je pense que c'est un gros problème et il faut vraiment faire quelque chose.'
cards.a: Il me semble que ce problème est préoccupant et qu'il convient d'agir. Formal register favors nuanced verbs (il me semble), precise adjectives (préoccupant) over vague ones (gros), and impersonal structures (il convient de) over blunt commands.
cards.n: Il convient de and il me semble que both sidestep je, which is what makes them sound academic rather than personal.

cards.q: State the number of questions and the time allowed for the Listening portion of the multiple-choice section.
cards.a: 25 questions in 40 minutes, drawn from three sets of audio sources (interviews, announcements or instructions, and presentations). Each audio plays twice.
cards.n: That is under two minutes per question including both playings - preview the questions the instant you see them.

cards.q: State the number of questions and the time allowed for the Reading portion of the multiple-choice section.
cards.a: 30 questions in 40 minutes, drawn from print sources such as articles, literary excerpts, letters, ads, charts, and tables.
cards.n: That is under 90 seconds per question on average - do not let one hard passage eat the time meant for two easy ones.

cards.q: State the total size of the multiple-choice section and what share of the exam score it represents.
cards.a: 55 questions in 80 minutes total (25 listening plus 30 reading), worth 50% of the exam score - the same weight as the three free-response tasks combined.
cards.n: The split matters for pacing: about 80 seconds per reading question, and no going back once the audio moves on.

cards.q: Decide: you cannot choose between two answer choices on a multiple-choice question after two read-throughs. Leave it blank, or guess?
cards.a: Always guess. AP exams carry no penalty for a wrong answer, so a blank and a wrong answer cost exactly the same: the point. A guess has a chance; a blank has none.
cards.n: Never leave a multiple-choice question unanswered on any AP exam, in any section.

cards.q: Explain what to do in the seconds after a new audio source's introduction appears, before the recording itself starts.
cards.a: Read the setup line and every visible question and answer choice. The setup usually names the speakers, the context, and the format, and can eliminate one answer choice outright before you hear a word.
cards.n: This previewing window is free information - it costs nothing and narrows what you are listening for.

cards.q: Explain how the digital Bluebook format changes your strategy for the reading passages, compared to reading on paper.
cards.a: You cannot flip pages or underline with a pen. Use the app's own highlight and note tools as you read, and expect to scroll: budget a few extra seconds per passage just for navigating the screen.
cards.n: Practice at least one full reading section inside Bluebook itself before exam day so scrolling and highlighting are automatic.

cards.q: Decide: it is minute 35 of the 40-minute Reading portion and four questions remain unanswered. What should you do?
cards.a: Answer every remaining question immediately, even with a blind guess, before time runs out - then use any leftover seconds to reconsider. An unanswered question is a guaranteed zero; a guessed one is not.
cards.n: There is no penalty for a wrong answer on this exam, which is why a blank is strictly worse than a guess.

cards.q: State three free-response task types that appear on many general AP language exams but do NOT appear on your redesigned French exam.
cards.a: The Email Reply (interpersonal writing), the Simulated Conversation (interpersonal speaking), and the stand-alone Cultural Comparison (presentational speaking) are all eliminated - the Project Presentation and Project Q&A absorbed those skills instead.
cards.n: Older French prep books and websites still drill these three tasks - do not spend study time preparing for them.

cards.q: Explain where the skill of comparing your own community to a Francophone one now shows up, now that the stand-alone Cultural Comparison task is gone.
cards.a: Inside the Project Presentation itself - a strong presentation includes at least one explicit comparison to your own community - and it can resurface in the Project Q&A if a question asks about your personal connection to the topic.
cards.n: The skill was not dropped, only relocated - keep practicing it.

cards.q: Explain how the 2027 redesign changed the way readers score each free-response task, compared with the old exam.
cards.a: The old holistic rubric (one single 0-5 band judging everything at once) is replaced by an analytic, point-based rubric: each task is scored dimension by dimension - task completion and development, organization, and language control - and the points are added together.
cards.n: An analytic rubric means one weak dimension does not automatically drag every other dimension down with it.

cards.q: State how the Argumentative Essay is scored on the 2027 rubric.
cards.a: On a published point-based analytic rubric worth 10 points, awarded across five separate categories rather than one holistic band. Broadly they cover task completion and argumentation (a defensible thesis, use of all three sources, a counterargument), organization and cohesion, and language control (vocabulary range, grammar accuracy, register).
cards.n: Points are awarded category by category, so a near-perfect thesis cannot rescue an essay that cites one source. Check the current CED for the exact category names.

cards.q: State how the Project Presentation is scored on the 2027 rubric.
cards.a: On a published point-based analytic rubric worth 11 points across five separate categories — the most heavily weighted single task on the exam, at 20% of the score. Broadly they cover task completion and development (answering the guiding question, cultural content, the comparison to your own community), organization and signposting, and language control (vocabulary, grammar, pronunciation, register).
cards.n: Nervous pauses cost language control, not task completion — a well-organised answer still earns its points there. Check the current CED for the exact category names.

cards.q: State how the Project Q&A is scored on the 2027 rubric, and how many questions it asks.
cards.a: Four pre-recorded questions, about 40 seconds to answer each, scored on a published point-based analytic rubric worth 9 points across several categories rather than one holistic band. They reward directly addressing the question asked, sustaining and elaborating the exchange, and language control under spontaneous timed conditions.
cards.n: Because it is spontaneous, language control is judged more forgivingly here than on the typed essay. Check the current CED for the exact category names.

cards.q: Define what 'maintains the exchange' means to an AP reader scoring the Project Q&A.
cards.a: Your answer directly and appropriately addresses what the question actually asked, in a way that keeps the exchange moving naturally - as opposed to ignoring the question, changing the subject, or giving an answer generic enough to fit any question.
cards.h: → definition, contrast with what fails it
cards.n: A fluent, grammatically perfect answer to the wrong question still fails to maintain the exchange.

cards.q: Define 'elaboration' the way an AP reader uses the term, and give the minimum shape that counts as elaborated.
cards.a: Going beyond a bare direct answer to add a reason, an example, a detail, or a consequence. The minimum: one full extra clause connected with a word like parce que, ce qui, or par exemple - not the same idea repeated in longer words.
cards.n: Repeating your answer in different words is not elaboration; readers are trained to spot the difference.

cards.q: Contrast a Project Q&A answer that merely answers with one that elaborates, for the question 'Pourquoi ce sujet vous intéresse-t-il ?'
cards.a: Merely answers: 'Ce sujet m'intéresse parce que c'est important.' Elaborates: 'Ce sujet m'intéresse parce que ma grand-mère a vécu cette réalité en Haïti, ce qui a rendu mes recherches personnelles dès le départ.'
cards.n: The elaborated version reuses the question's structure and adds one concrete, personal detail - exactly what raises the score.

cards.q: Donne trois formules de haut niveau pour exprimer une conséquence ou un résultat.
cards.a: Par conséquent, ... / Ainsi, ... / De ce fait, ...
cards.n: Vary these across an essay instead of repeating donc every time - repetition reads as thin vocabulary.

cards.q: Donne trois formules de haut niveau pour introduire une cause ou une explication.
cards.a: Étant donné que... / Dans la mesure où... / Cela s'explique par le fait que...
cards.n: Étant donné que and dans la mesure où both take the indicative, not the subjunctive - a common student error is adding one out of habit.

cards.q: Donne deux structures pour formuler une hypothèse ou une condition dans un essai argumentatif, avec un exemple pour chacune.
cards.a: Si + présent, ... futur : Si cette tendance se poursuit, la situation s'aggravera. / À condition que + subjonctif : ... à condition que les autorités agissent rapidement.
cards.n: Si always takes the indicative, never the subjunctive - mixing them (si ce soit) is one of the most common formal-register errors.

cards.q: Donne trois formules de haut niveau pour souligner l'importance d'un point.
cards.a: Il est primordial de... / Il importe de souligner que... / Ce point mérite une attention particulière.
cards.n: Il est primordial de + infinitif keeps the sentence impersonal and formal - avoid je pense que c'est important.

cards.q: Cite trois mots utiles pour un essai sur le monde du travail.
cards.a: le télétravail (remote work) / la précarité (job insecurity) / le déséquilibre vie professionnelle-vie privée (work-life imbalance).
cards.n: La précarité is the word graders notice, and its adjective is précaire, as in un emploi précaire.

cards.q: Cite trois mots utiles pour un essai sur l'identité et l'immigration.
cards.a: l'intégration (integration) / le multiculturalisme (multiculturalism) / le déracinement (uprooting, loss of one's roots).
cards.n: Le déracinement is the high-value word here; pair it with les racines and se sentir déraciné for range.

cards.q: Cite trois mots utiles pour un essai sur l'éducation.
cards.a: la réussite scolaire (academic success) / le décrochage scolaire (dropping out) / l'inégalité des chances (unequal opportunity).
cards.n: Le décrochage comes from décrocher, to drop out, and the student concerned is un décrocheur or une décrocheuse.

cards.q: Cite trois mots utiles pour un essai sur l'environnement, différents de ceux d'un répertoire de base (gaspillage, écologique).
cards.a: l'empreinte carbone (carbon footprint) / la transition énergétique (energy transition) / la biodiversité (biodiversity).
cards.n: L'empreinte carbone is feminine, and its usual verbs are réduire, compenser and calculer son empreinte.

cards.q: Explain why using the subjunctive correctly after expressions like il faut que and bien que raises your language-control score, beyond simple grammatical accuracy.
cards.a: The subjunctive is a marker of grammatical range and formal register - readers are trained to notice varied structures, not just accuracy. An essay using only the indicative reads as simple even when it is error-free.
cards.n: Bien que forces the subjunctive even though the fact conceded is objectively true - a frequent slip.

cards.q: Decide: should you ever address the audience as tu instead of vous in the Project Presentation or Project Q&A?
cards.a: No. Both are addressed to an unknown evaluator in an academic context - vous is the only appropriate choice unless a prompt explicitly has you quoting yourself speaking to a specific, informal person.
cards.n: Slipping into tu drags the wrong verb endings along with it, so one lapse tends to spread through the whole answer.

cards.q: Donne deux formules pour exprimer une certitude nuancée, ni trop timide ni trop absolue.
cards.a: Il est fort probable que + indicatif... / Tout porte à croire que...
cards.n: Avoid both je suis sûr que (too absolute for an argumentative essay) and peut-être (too weak) - these two sit in between.

cards.q: Donne trois formules pour relier une donnée chiffrée à son explication, sans répéter 'ce qui montre que'.
cards.a: Ce chiffre traduit... / Cela reflète... / Ces données témoignent de...
cards.n: Varying the link-verb (traduit, reflète, témoigne de) instead of always ce qui montre que raises the vocabulary-range signal readers look for.

cards.q: Sujet : « Le télétravail profite-t-il davantage aux employés ou aux entreprises ? » Écris une phrase de thèse qui prend clairement position.
cards.a: Nous soutiendrons que, malgré les avantages qu'il procure aux entreprises, le télétravail profite avant tout aux employés en leur rendant un temps et une autonomie précieux.
cards.n: Notice davantage from the prompt reappears as avant tout, showing you engaged with the exact question asked.

cards.q: Sujet : « Les jeunes doivent-ils apprendre une langue étrangère dès l'école primaire ? » Cite la source audio dans une phrase qui l'interprète, pas seulement qui la résume.
cards.a: Dans l'enregistrement, la linguiste affirme que l'apprentissage précoce double les chances de bilinguisme réel, ce qui suggère que retarder l'enseignement des langues revient à fermer une fenêtre biologique.
cards.n: Ce qui suggère que is the interpretation clause - without it, the sentence would only summarize the source.

cards.q: Sujet : « Le patrimoine culturel doit-il primer sur le développement économique ? » Écris, en une seule phrase, une concession suivie d'un contre-argument.
cards.a: Certes, le développement économique crée des emplois indispensables, mais sacrifier un patrimoine irremplaçable pour un gain à court terme prive les générations futures de leur mémoire collective.
cards.n: Certes followed by mais is the standard concession pair; il est vrai que and bien que plus the subjunctive also work.

cards.q: Sujet : « L'intelligence artificielle menace-t-elle plus d'emplois qu'elle n'en crée ? » Écris la phrase de conclusion, en élargissant vers une perspective plus large.
cards.a: En somme, si l'intelligence artificielle transformera inévitablement le marché du travail, c'est la volonté politique de former les travailleurs qui déterminera si cette transformation est une menace ou une opportunité.
cards.n: The opening restates the thesis in new words before pivoting outward - copying the thesis verbatim is a common weak-conclusion mistake.

cards.q: Fix the register error and explain it: 'Je crois que les gens sont un peu fatigués des réseaux sociaux, tu sais.'
cards.a: Il semble que les individus éprouvent une certaine lassitude à l'égard des réseaux sociaux. This removes the direct address (tu sais) and vague filler (un peu), and replaces the casual opener (je crois) with an impersonal, formal structure.
cards.n: Tu sais and other direct-address fillers are the fastest way to sound conversational in a task that requires formal register.

cards.q: Write a French sentence for an argumentative essay that uses the subjunctive after 'bien que' to concede a point about globalization.
cards.a: Bien que la mondialisation ait permis un accès sans précédent aux biens et aux idées, elle a aussi creusé les inégalités entre pays riches et pays pauvres.
cards.n: Bien que always takes the subjunctive, even though the fact conceded is objectively true - switching to the indicative here is a frequent error.

cards.q: Decide: your essay's second body paragraph is running long and you are at minute 30 of 40. Finish developing this point fully, or cut it short to guarantee a conclusion?
cards.a: Cut it short and move to your conclusion. An essay with a strong thesis, evidence, and a genuine ending outscores one with a brilliant but unfinished middle and no conclusion - task completion covers the whole essay.
cards.n: Rehearse a two-sentence conclusion you can deploy under pressure, so the ending never depends on spare time.

cards.q: Write one French sentence that cites the print-article source (source numéro 1) using a verb other than affirmer or soutenir.
cards.a: La source numéro 1 met en lumière le fait que les petites exploitations agricoles peinent à survivre face à la concurrence industrielle.
cards.n: Verb variety across your three citations (met en lumière, souligne, dénonce, nuance) is exactly the vocabulary range readers reward.

cards.q: Identify the single most common way students lose the task-completion point on the Argumentative Essay, given how the task is structured.
cards.a: Summarizing the three sources' positions without ever stating and defending the writer's own position - a well-informed survey of the debate is not an argument.
cards.n: The prompt's own verb - usually développer une position, prendre position, or soutenir un point de vue - always demands a stance, not a summary.

cards.q: Sujet : « Les grandes villes doivent-elles limiter la voiture individuelle ? » Écris la première phrase de l'introduction, qui présente le sujet sans donner ta thèse.
cards.a: La place de la voiture individuelle dans les grandes villes suscite un débat de plus en plus vif entre partisans de la mobilité durable et défenseurs de la liberté de circulation.
cards.n: Opening on the debate rather than your answer is what the rubric calls framing; the thesis belongs in the next sentence.

cards.q: Write the guiding-question sentence (part of the roughly 20-second hook) for a Project Presentation about the decline of regional languages in France.
cards.a: Comment se fait-il qu'une langue parlée par des millions de Français il y a un siècle risque aujourd'hui de disparaître complètement ?
cards.n: Comment se fait-il que takes the subjunctive, so the question frames the project and shows off a structure at once.

cards.q: Write one sentence of cultural context (part of the roughly 40-second block) for a Project Presentation about Carnaval in Guadeloupe.
cards.a: Le Carnaval guadeloupéen, hérité à la fois des traditions africaines et des célébrations catholiques coloniales, occupe une place centrale dans l'identité antillaise depuis le 17e siècle.
cards.n: Naming a concrete origin and date signals research depth, not just general knowledge.

cards.q: Write a transition sentence moving from your first developed point to your second, for a project about food deserts in rural Quebec.
cards.a: Si l'accès limité aux commerces alimentaires touche d'abord la santé physique des habitants, il fragilise également le lien social qui se tissait autrefois autour du marché du village.
cards.n: The transition names both points explicitly instead of just saying deuxièmement - that is what makes structure audible to a listener.

cards.q: Write a one-sentence comparison to your own community for a project about urban gardening initiatives in Dakar.
cards.a: Contrairement à Dakar, où les jardins urbains répondent surtout à un besoin alimentaire, dans ma ville ils relèvent davantage d'un choix écologique que d'une nécessité.
cards.n: A real comparison names a difference or similarity explicitly - describing your own community without relating it back does not count.

cards.q: Decide: your rehearsed Project Presentation consistently runs to 3 minutes 40 seconds. Speak faster to fit, or cut content?
cards.a: Cut content. Speeding up to fit hurts pronunciation and intonation, which are scored - losing your weakest example keeps the delivery natural and controlled.
cards.n: Cut the weakest example outright rather than trimming everywhere, since even trimming leaves every point underdeveloped.

cards.q: Write the closing sentence for a Project Presentation about water scarcity in the Maghreb, answering the guiding question in one line.
cards.a: Voilà pourquoi la gestion de l'eau au Maghreb n'est pas seulement un défi technique, mais un choix de société qui engage l'avenir de toute la région.
cards.n: Voilà pourquoi signals a conclusion audibly, which matters when the listener has no paragraph breaks to see.

cards.q: Explain why a Project Presentation that only describes facts about the topic, without returning to the guiding question, loses points even with flawless French.
cards.a: Task completion requires the presentation to answer its own question, not just inform about the topic - description without an answer leaves the task incomplete no matter how accurate the language is.
cards.n: Task completion is scored separately from language, so flawless French cannot rescue an unanswered question.

cards.q: Rewrite this flat, list-like sentence as a more engaging cultural-context sentence: 'Il y a beaucoup de festivals de musique en Afrique de l'Ouest.'
cards.a: Chaque année, des festivals comme le Festival au Désert rassemblent des dizaines de milliers de spectateurs venus célébrer une scène musicale ouest-africaine en pleine effervescence.
cards.n: A named, specific example almost always outperforms a vague generalization on both content and vocabulary range.

cards.q: Decide: should your Project Presentation end on a question left open for the audience, the way a strong essay conclusion can?
cards.a: No, avoid it here. The task rewards answering your own guiding question decisively; ending on an open question can read as an incomplete task rather than as sophistication.
cards.n: This is one place where a technique that works well in the Argumentative Essay conclusion works against you.

cards.q: Question enregistrée : « Quelle a été la partie la plus difficile de vos recherches ? » Donne un modèle de réponse de 40 secondes en trois mouvements.
cards.a: La partie la plus difficile a été de trouver des sources fiables en français sur un sujet local. Beaucoup d'articles étaient en anglais, ce qui m'a obligé à consulter des journaux régionaux directement, comme Le Nouvelliste en Haïti, pour vérifier mes informations.
cards.n: Notice the answer reuses difficile from the question and closes with a specific, named source.

cards.q: Question enregistrée : « En quoi votre sujet est-il lié à l'un des thèmes du cours ? » Donne un modèle de réponse qui commence par une réponse directe.
cards.a: Mon sujet est lié au thème de la famille et de la communauté, car j'étudie comment les associations de quartier à Marseille recréent un tissu social pour les nouveaux immigrés.
cards.n: Naming the exact course theme in your first sentence is a fast, unambiguous way to show task completion.

cards.q: Question enregistrée : « Que répondriez-vous à quelqu'un qui pense que votre sujet n'est pas vraiment important ? » Réponds en gérant poliment le désaccord.
cards.a: Je comprends ce point de vue, mais je dirais que ce sujet touche directement la vie quotidienne de millions de francophones, ce qui le rend, à mon sens, tout à fait pertinent.
cards.n: Je comprends ce point de vue, mais... lets you disagree without sounding combative - exactly the register the task expects.

cards.q: Tu ne trouves pas le mot exact pour 'greenwashing' pendant ta réponse. Donne une phrase de circonlocution en français pour exprimer cette idée sans le mot.
cards.a: C'est quand une entreprise prétend être écologique dans sa publicité, alors qu'en réalité ses actions ne changent presque rien pour l'environnement.
cards.n: C'est quand is the plainest circumlocution opener; c'est une sorte de and cela consiste à work just as well.

cards.q: Question enregistrée : « Si vous deviez recommencer ce projet, que feriez-vous différemment ? » Réponds en une phrase avec le conditionnel passé.
cards.a: Si j'avais eu plus de temps, j'aurais interviewé directement des habitants de la région au lieu de me limiter aux articles, ce qui aurait rendu mes exemples encore plus concrets.
cards.n: si + plus-que-parfait takes the conditionnel passé (j'aurais interviewé). Pairing the conditionnel passé with 'si je devais' mixes two different sequences.

cards.q: Decide: the recorded question restates something your Personalized Project Reference already covers almost word for word. Should your answer just recite that part of the PPR?
cards.a: No - reformulate it in your own spoken words and add one new detail or angle the PPR does not already state. A near-verbatim recitation sounds memorized and does not demonstrate spontaneous language control.
cards.n: The Q&A is scored partly on spontaneity, so a paraphrase with one fresh detail beats a faithful quotation.

cards.q: Question enregistrée : « Quelles sources avez-vous utilisées et pourquoi leur avez-vous fait confiance ? » Donne la première phrase de ta réponse.
cards.a: J'ai principalement utilisé des articles de Radio-Canada et une étude universitaire québécoise, parce que ce sont des sources reconnues et directement liées à la région que j'étudiais.
cards.n: Naming a Francophone source rather than a translated English one also shows the cultural grounding the rubric rewards.

cards.q: Contrast a Project Q&A answer that goes off-topic with one that stays on-topic, for the question « Comment ce projet a-t-il changé votre point de vue ? »
cards.a: Off-topic: describes the project's subject again without mentioning any change in the student. On-topic: 'Avant mes recherches, je pensais que..., mais j'ai découvert que..., ce qui a changé ma manière de voir la question.'
cards.n: The question asks specifically about change in you - restating facts about the topic, however accurate, does not maintain the exchange.

cards.q: Question enregistrée : « Quelle question resterait à approfondir si vous aviez plus de temps ? » Donne un modèle de réponse complète.
cards.a: Il resterait à approfondir l'impact économique de cette initiative sur le long terme, car mes sources ne couvraient que les deux premières années du programme, ce qui limite mes conclusions.
cards.n: This question type rewards intellectual honesty about your project's limits - naming one is a strength here, not a weakness.

cards.q: Decide: 15 seconds into your 40-second Project Q&A answer, you realize you misunderstood the question. Stop and restart, or adjust course mid-answer?
cards.a: Adjust course mid-answer with a natural bridge - ou plutôt, pour répondre plus précisément... - and pivot. Stopping and restarting wastes seconds you cannot get back and creates dead air, which hurts more than a visible self-correction.
cards.n: A smooth self-correction is itself a recognized communication strategy, not a deduction.

cards.q: Question enregistrée : « Recommanderiez-vous ce sujet de recherche à un autre élève ? Pourquoi ? » Réponds en 40 secondes avec les trois mouvements.
cards.a: Oui, je le recommanderais, car ce sujet reste peu étudié malgré son importance actuelle. Un autre élève pourrait par exemple explorer l'aspect économique que je n'ai pas eu le temps de traiter, ce qui prolongerait naturellement mes propres recherches.
cards.n: Recommanderiez-vous is in the conditional, so the answer echoes it: je le recommanderais, not je le recommande.

cards.q: Élabore cette réponse trop courte pour qu'elle compte comme une réponse développée : « Oui, mon sujet est important. »
cards.a: Oui, mon sujet est important, parce qu'il touche à une question d'actualité que peu de gens connaissent en dehors de la région concernée, ce qui en fait, je pense, un angle vraiment original.
cards.n: Parce que followed by a relative clause is the quickest way to stretch a one-line answer without padding it.

cards.q: Decide: during the Project Q&A, the recorded question includes a word you don't recognize at all. Ask to skip it, stay silent, or answer your best guess at its meaning?
cards.a: There is no option to skip or ask for clarification - answer based on your best guess at the question's general topic, staying as close as possible to your project. A confident, on-topic attempt beats silence every time.
cards.n: Unlike a live conversation, a recorded prompt cannot be asked to repeat or clarify - you get one hearing.

cards.q: Decide, from context: in 'Les négociations ont finalement abouti à un accord,' does 'abouti' suggest failure or success?
cards.a: Success. Aboutir à means to result in or lead successfully to an outcome - here the negotiations succeeded in reaching an agreement, not merely ended inconclusively.
cards.n: Aboutir on its own can simply mean to end up somewhere; the sense of success comes with à plus a result.

cards.q: From context, in 'Le gouvernement a dû réviser sa copie après les critiques,' does 'réviser sa copie' mean literally rewrite an exam paper, or something else?
cards.a: It is an idiom meaning to go back to the drawing board or rework a plan. In a news context about government policy, no literal exam paper is involved.
cards.n: Idiomatic expressions built on ordinary words (copie, chantier, terrain) are a frequent reading-section trap.

cards.q: State a common trap in Section-I audio sources that involve numbers or statistics, and how to avoid it.
cards.a: A speaker states a statistic and then immediately qualifies or contrasts it (mais ce chiffre a doublé depuis, or contrairement à l'an dernier). Note the qualifier, not just the first number you hear.
cards.n: Listen for the pivot words mais, pourtant, en revanche and contrairement à, which announce the qualifier.

cards.q: Explain how to handle an unfamiliar word in a reading passage that you cannot infer from the immediate sentence.
cards.a: Keep reading to the end of the sentence or paragraph - French often restates or exemplifies a new idea shortly after introducing it. Reading forward for confirmation beats stopping to guess in isolation.
cards.n: French flags a restatement with c'est-à-dire, autrement dit and notamment, so those words announce a free definition.

cards.q: Decide: a reading-section question asks for a passage's main idea, and two answer choices both seem partially true. Which one wins?
cards.a: The one that covers the passage as a whole, not just one paragraph or example. Main-idea questions test whether a detail was mistaken for the whole - a choice built from a single supporting example is the trap.
cards.n: The French stems to recognise are quelle est l'idée principale and le passage traite surtout de.

cards.q: State why skimming a print source's introductory line before reading the full passage is worth the extra seconds it costs.
cards.a: It usually names the publication, the date, and the genre, setting your expectations for register and purpose before you start reading - context you would otherwise reconstruct sentence by sentence.
cards.n: That line is in French and often abbreviated, so learn the usual formulas: extrait de, adapté de, publié dans.

cards.q: Decide: with 5 minutes left in the 40-minute essay period, you have not written your conclusion. Finish body paragraph three's last detail, or jump to the conclusion?
cards.a: Jump to the conclusion. An essay that stops mid-paragraph with no conclusion looks incomplete to a reader; a shorter but finished conclusion protects the organization score even if body paragraph three is thinner.
cards.n: Organization is a scored dimension in its own right, so a visible ending protects points a thin paragraph cannot.

cards.q: State what to check in the very last minute of the Argumentative Essay, after the conclusion is written.
cards.a: A dedicated citation check: confirm all three sources are explicitly named somewhere in the essay. It is the single fastest point to lose and the fastest to verify.
cards.n: Sources are named in French, as in selon la source numéro un or d'après le tableau, not with English quotation marks.

cards.q: Explain the single biggest difference in how much you can revise between the Argumentative Essay and the two speaking tasks.
cards.a: The essay is typed, so you can reread and fix errors before time runs out. The Project Presentation and Project Q&A are recorded once you begin speaking - there is no rerecording, so a spoken slip stands unless you self-correct out loud in the moment.
cards.n: A spoken self-correction such as je veux dire reads as control rather than error, so say it out loud when you slip.

cards.q: Identify the most common near-miss on the Project Presentation's task-completion dimension, beyond simply running short on time.
cards.a: Presenting interesting facts about the topic without ever stating or answering a guiding question - informative but not argumentative, so it reads as a report rather than a presentation with a point.
cards.n: The fix takes one sentence: state the question in the hook, then answer it explicitly in the conclusion.

cards.q: Identify the most common near-miss on the Project Q&A's task-completion dimension.
cards.a: Giving a fluent, well-developed answer to a slightly different question than the one actually asked - often because the student prepared an answer in advance and forces the question to fit it.
cards.n: Buy yourself a second to listen properly by opening with a short echo of the question before answering it.

cards.q: Contrast what 'organization' rewards on the Argumentative Essay versus on the Project Presentation.
cards.a: On the essay, organization means visible paragraph structure and written connectors (cependant, par conséquent). On the presentation, it means audible signposting in speech (tout d'abord, ensuite, enfin) since the listener cannot see paragraph breaks.
cards.n: Spoken signposts work precisely because the listener cannot rewind, so say them clearly and pause after each.

skills.name: Use language that aligns with the communicative purpose and context.
Make communication comprehensible for the intended audience.
Share ideas, information, and opinions about familiar and researched topics.
Make connections within and across cultures.
